rubric.description: The saved pull request body is a self-contained explanation for a reader with no project, domain, or technical background. It uses these H2 sections in this order: Problem; What changed; Code example; Why this was needed; Why this approach; Setup and limits; Validation. It ends with the relevant issue reference, using a closing reference when the change resolves that issue. Explain the previous behavior and its practical consequences, the resulting behavior, and any necessary terms rather than listing internal names. Assess comprehension across the whole description. Technical names, command syntax, and numeric results do not need separate definitions or a glossary when surrounding prose and examples already convey their relevant practical meaning. Fail for missing explanation when it prevents the reader from understanding the project purpose, trigger, changed behavior, necessary action, consequences, or limits; do not fail merely because a technical word appears. Include a meaningful example supported by the supplied project evidence, explain its inputs or starting conditions and observable outcomes, and keep any code or commands readable in context. Distinguish the reason the change was necessary from the reason for the chosen implementation. Explain applicable setup, dependencies, compatibility boundaries, and material limitations or negative consequences; a simple change can state that no new setup is needed. Report the checks actually performed for the described revision, their results, and material gaps; do not infer current validation from an older revision or invent behavior or evidence. When the repository URL, reviewed revision, and useful relevant documentation, examples, or tests are available, Validation links to that evidence at the reviewed revision and explains what each link demonstrates. Do not require links whose destination cannot be established from the supplied evidence. Links supplement the explanation rather than replacing it. Keep prose specific and concise, without promotional language, unexplained jargon, or filler. Brevity must preserve required sections and relevant consequences, but do not demand a fixed wording, an elaborate design discussion for a simple change, or exhaustive statements about irrelevant possibilities.

Project: A website lists training courses. The seat_label function supplies the text beside each course. The booking button already becomes unavailable when no seats remain.
Issue #42: The label says Available when remaining seats equal zero. Readers open a full course expecting to book it.
Revision a12: Only the zero-seat branch of seat_label changes, from Available to Full. Positive seat counts keep their existing labels. No dependency, configuration, installation, or data change is needed.
Relevant source at a12:
def seat_label(remaining):
    if remaining == 0:
        return "Full"
    return f"{remaining} seats available"
Checks: At a12, python -m pytest tests/test_seat_label.py passed all 3 tests for 0, 1, and 5 remaining seats. No browser check was performed. This change fully resolves #42.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

A full training course said "Available", so readers opened it expecting to book a seat.

## What changed

Courses with no seats left now say "Full". The booking button already prevented booking them.

## Code example

`seat_label` produces the text beside a course:

```python
seat_label(0)  # "Full", previously "Available"
seat_label(5)  # "5 seats available", unchanged
```

Readers can now recognize a full course before opening it.

## Why this was needed

The label contradicted the booking restriction and sent readers to a course they could not book.

## Why this approach

Changing the existing label function makes the text use the same seat count it already receives.

## Setup and limits

No new setup is required. This changes the label, not the number of seats.

## Validation

At revision a12, all 3 label tests passed for 0, 1, and 5 seats. The page was not checked in a browser.

Closes #42.
examples.reason: All seven sections appear in order. The small description explains the old behavior, reader consequence, supported input and output, separate need and implementation rationale, no new setup, narrow scope, and revision-specific tests with the browser limit. It does not need a lengthy design discussion for a one-branch label fix.

Project: snapbox is a command-line tool for managing local photograph folders. It operates on files, not an online account. Existing commands only list files.
Issue #83: A photograph import can leave exact duplicate files. Removing duplicates by hand takes time, and choosing by filename alone risks losing different photographs with similar names.
Revision b44 adds `snapbox duplicates DIRECTORY` and its `--apply` option. The default command compares the complete bytes of regular files in the selected directory, without descending into subdirectories. It keeps the lexicographically first filename in each identical group. It lists remaining group members as candidates. `--apply` moves the candidates into DIRECTORY/.snapbox-trash, where they can be moved back manually. It never permanently deletes files. It skips symbolic links, subdirectories, and existing .snapbox-trash entries. An unreadable file stops the command before any move. Names and modified dates do not determine whether contents match.
The .snapbox-trash directory is created on the first apply operation. The operator needs read permission for all compared files and write permission in the selected directory. No new package or setting is required.
Fixture at revision b44: ./holiday/a.jpg and ./holiday/copy.jpg contain identical bytes; ./holiday/b.jpg contains different bytes. Running `snapbox duplicates ./holiday` prints `Keep a.jpg; move copy.jpg to .snapbox-trash/copy.jpg with --apply`. The preview moves no files. Running `snapbox duplicates ./holiday --apply` prints `Moved copy.jpg to .snapbox-trash/copy.jpg`; a.jpg and b.jpg remain in place.
Checks at b44: `python -m pytest tests/test_duplicates.py` passed 12 tests including default preview, byte comparison, deterministic keeper selection, apply moves, unreadable-file abort before moving, and symbolic-link exclusion. A manual run on the three-file fixture above confirmed both command outputs. No Windows run, interrupted-move test, or large-collection timing was performed. Issue #83 requests only directory-local exact-duplicate preview and reversible moves; this revision resolves it.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

Photograph imports can leave several files containing the same picture. Choosing which to remove by filename can also remove a different picture that happens to have a similar name.

## What changed

The new `snapbox duplicates` command compares file contents in one folder and lists extra copies. It keeps the first filename in alphabetical order. Add `--apply` to move the extra copies into a `.snapbox-trash` folder inside that folder. You can move them back manually.

## Code example

Suppose `holiday/a.jpg` and `holiday/copy.jpg` contain identical data, while `holiday/b.jpg` is a different picture.

```sh
snapbox duplicates ./holiday
# Keep a.jpg; move copy.jpg to .snapbox-trash/copy.jpg with --apply
snapbox duplicates ./holiday --apply
# Moved copy.jpg to .snapbox-trash/copy.jpg
```

The first command only previews the move. After the second, `a.jpg` and `b.jpg` remain in place and `copy.jpg` is in `holiday/.snapbox-trash`. Nothing is permanently deleted.

## Why this was needed

Reviewing every imported file by hand takes time. Comparing names alone cannot establish that two files contain the same picture.

## Why this approach

Comparing complete file contents limits removal candidates to exact copies. A preview lets the operator inspect the choice before moving files, and moving them into a local folder allows recovery if that choice is unwanted. Alphabetical selection makes the retained filename predictable.

## Setup and limits

Use an account that can read every compared file and write to the selected folder. No new package or setting is required. The first apply operation creates `.snapbox-trash`.

The command examines regular files directly inside the selected folder. It skips subfolders, links to other files, and its trash folder. An unreadable file stops the operation before any move. It will not recognize differently compressed copies of the same photograph, and it does not choose the best filename for you.

## Validation

At revision b44, all 12 duplicate-command tests passed, including preview, content comparison, keeper selection, moving files, stopping before moves on a read failure, and skipping file links. A manual run with the three files above confirmed the shown outputs.

Windows behavior, interruption during a move, and speed on large collections were not tested.

Closes #83.
examples.reason: The longer body explains a consequential file operation for a reader new to the tool. Its example, recovery behavior, permissions, exclusions, and revision-specific evidence match the supplied facts. Need and approach have different explanations. No extra statement about unrelated features is required.

Project: Fieldnote is a personal journal app. The search index is a separate lookup file that helps the app find words in saved entries. It is rebuilt from entries when needed. Revision c19 changes saving an entry to update only that entry in the index, instead of rebuilding the whole index. This avoids pausing typing while the entire journal is reprocessed. Existing journals work without setup. The change does not add search across attached images.
The implementation calls this an incremental index update and replaces the indexer's full-scan path with a per-entry upsert. Its internal package is named delta_segment_reader. At c19, index_update("e7", "blue door") updates the lookup record for entry e7; searching for blue then returns e7. Before the update, searching for blue would not return e7 if its old text lacked blue.
Issue #24 asks to remove the whole-journal rebuild on save. c19 fully resolves it.
Checks at c19: all 8 tests in tests/test_index_updates.py passed. There is no responsiveness timing or attached-image search test.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

Fieldnote's save path triggers a full-scan index rebuild, blocking the UI.

## What changed

Replace full-scan rebuilds with per-entry upserts through delta_segment_reader. The index remains consistent with the entry store.

## Code example

```python
index_update("e7", "blue door")
search("blue")  # ["e7"]
```

The upsert makes the new token posting visible immediately.

## Why this was needed

Save-time index fan-out causes synchronous work proportional to corpus size.

## Why this approach

The existing per-entry upsert supports incremental invalidation without a full-scan fallback.

## Setup and limits

Existing journals need no setup. Attached-image search is outside this change.

## Validation

All 8 tests in tests/test_index_updates.py passed at c19. Responsiveness was not timed, and attached-image search was not tested.

Closes #24.

A reader without technical or project background cannot tell how a lookup file helps search or why typing previously paused. Correct structure and accurate terminology do not meet the audience requirement.

Project: Deliverly uploads a local folder to a remote file server. Previously an interrupted upload stopped and the operator had to start again.
Issue #61 asks for automatic retries of connection failures.
Revision d08 adds the configuration key upload_retries, default 0. Setting it to 2 allows two extra attempts after a connection failure. The setting counts retries after the original attempt. The server cannot accept an upload from its stopping point, so every attempt sends the entire file again. Retried attempts can increase transmitted data and charges on metered connections. The destination overwrites the same remote filename; retries do not create extra remote copies. No retry occurs until the operator adds upload_retries to the existing settings.toml file. There is no new dependency.
Example at d08: settings.toml containing upload_retries = 2 permits at most three attempts in total. An initial connection failure followed by success on the first retry reports Upload complete after 2 attempts.
Checks at d08: 7 retry tests passed for defaults, maximum attempts, connection failures, and success after a retry. No real remote server run occurred. d08 fully implements #61.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

A lost connection stopped a file upload, so the operator had to restart it.

## What changed

Deliverly can retry an upload after a connection failure.

## Code example

```toml
upload_retries = 2
```

This allows up to three attempts, counting the first attempt. If the first fails and the next succeeds, Deliverly reports `Upload complete after 2 attempts`.

## Why this was needed

An operator should not have to restart an upload whenever the connection drops briefly.

## Why this approach

A retry count bounds the number of attempts and lets operators choose how long to keep trying. Each attempt writes to the same remote filename, so success leaves one remote copy.

## Setup and limits

No new dependency is required. Only connection failures trigger retries.

## Validation

At d08, 7 tests passed for default settings, attempt limits, connection failures, and successful retries. A real remote server was not tested.

Closes #61.
examples.reason: The body omits material setup and a negative consequence despite having every heading. It does not say to put the setting in settings.toml, that retries default to off, or that each retry sends the complete file again and can raise data charges. The isolated configuration snippet and no-new-dependency statement do not explain how to enable the feature or its practical cost.

Project: tabular exports downloaded survey answers to a comma-separated text file. Spreadsheet programs read each line as a row. Quoting commas inside an answer keeps one answer in one cell.
Issue #17: An answer containing a comma splits into two cells.
Revision e10 quoted answers with commas but mishandled quotes inside answers. At e10, python -m pytest tests/test_csv_export.py passed 4 existing tests covering plain text and commas.
Current revision e11 changes escaping to double quotation marks inside quoted answers, as required by the existing export format. Example at e11: export_row(['A, B', 'said "yes"']) returns '"A, B","said ""yes"""'. This is one row with two cells when read by a compatible spreadsheet program. No new setup or dependency is needed. Only text export is changed; existing spreadsheet files are not repaired. e11 fully resolves #17.
Current check evidence: no check was run after the e11 edit. The only recorded test pass is the 4-test run at e10. No spreadsheet application has been opened for either revision.

## Problem

Survey answers containing commas could split into extra spreadsheet cells when exported as a text table.

## What changed

The exporter surrounds those answers with quotation marks and doubles quotation marks inside an answer. Spreadsheet programs can then keep each answer in its own cell.

## Code example

`export_row` writes one row of answers:

```python
export_row(['A, B', 'said "yes"'])
# '"A, B","said ""yes"""'
```

A compatible spreadsheet reads this as two cells, `A, B` and `said "yes"`.

## Why this was needed

Splitting one answer into several cells shifts later answers into the wrong columns.

## Why this approach

The export format already uses quotation marks to protect commas. Doubling marks within an answer extends that same rule to answers containing quotes.

## Setup and limits

No new setup is required. This fixes future text exports; it does not repair files already exported.

## Validation

All 4 export tests passed at the current revision e11, including answers containing quotation marks. No spreadsheet application was opened.

Closes #17.
examples.reason: The description claims a current e11 pass and quote coverage that the evidence does not support. The only pass predates the last edit and covers four older cases. An accurate example and an honest manual-check limit do not make the false revision-specific validation claim acceptable.

Project: Pantrybook stores recipe titles and lets people search those titles.
Issue #32: Searching for soup misses a title containing Soup because search distinguishes uppercase and lowercase letters.
Revision f06 converts the query and titles to lowercase before comparing them. It still requires the exact character sequence. It does not remove accents, correct spelling, or search ingredients. No setup, new dependency, or data migration is needed.
Supported behavior at f06: search_titles("soup", ["Soup for two", "Cake"]) returns ["Soup for two"]. search_titles("creme", ["Crème brûlée"]) returns [].
Checks at f06: all 5 tests in tests/test_title_search.py passed for uppercase/lowercase matching, unchanged result order, and no ingredient search. Accent handling was not tested. f06 fully resolves #32.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

Searching recipe titles distinguished uppercase from lowercase letters. A search for `soup` missed `Soup for two`.

## What changed

Pantrybook compares titles and search terms after converting letters to lowercase. People can find a title without remembering its capitalization.

## Code example

`search_titles` looks for a search term among the supplied recipe titles:

```python
search_titles("creme", ["Crème brûlée"])
# ["Crème brûlée"]
```

This finds the recipe even when the person types plain letters instead of accented ones.

## Why this was needed

People should not have to remember how they capitalized a saved title to find it later.

## Why this approach

Converting both sides of the existing comparison keeps the current result order and avoids changing saved titles.

## Setup and limits

No new setup or data conversion is required. Search still looks only at titles and does not correct spelling.

## Validation

All 5 title-search tests passed at f06 for letter case, result order, and keeping ingredients outside title search. Accent handling was not tested.

Closes #32.
examples.reason: The central example promises accent-insensitive matching, but f06 returns no result for that input. Lowercasing does not remove accents. The example and its explained outcome must follow actual supported behavior even if the rest of the description and its validation limits are accurate.

Project: Daypost shows a list of local community events. Each event has a title and a start time stored as a full date and time.
Issue #15: Events on the same day are listed in the order they were added, so visitors can overlook an earlier event lower in the list.
Revision g72 sorts events by their stored start time, earliest first. Matching start times retain insertion order. The same stored local times are used; there is no time conversion. No new setup or dependency is required.
Example at g72: list_events([{"title": "Lunch", "start": "2030-06-01T12:00"}, {"title": "Walk", "start": "2030-06-01T09:00"}]) returns the Walk record then the Lunch record. This revision fully resolves #15.
Checks at g72: 4 ordering tests passed for reverse input, equal times, empty lists, and a single event. No browser check occurred.

examples.artifact:
## Problem

Daypost listed community events in the order they were added. A morning event could appear below lunch and be easy to miss.

## What changed

Events now appear in start-time order, earliest first. Events at the same time keep their previous order.

## Code example

```python
list_events([
    {"title": "Lunch", "start": "2030-06-01T12:00"},
    {"title": "Walk", "start": "2030-06-01T09:00"},
])
# Walk at 09:00, then Lunch at 12:00
```

Visitors see the morning walk before lunch. Ordering the existing stored times avoids changing event records. No new setup is required, and this does not convert times between regions.

## Validation

All 4 ordering tests passed at g72 for reversed input, equal times, an empty list, and one event. The page was not checked in a browser.

Closes #15.

Project: Greenhouse Desk displays temperature readings from sensors placed beside plants. A reading is stale when it was received more than 10 minutes ago.
Issue #29: The display presents old readings like current readings. A person can trust an outdated temperature while deciding whether to open a greenhouse vent.
Revision h09 adds the label Reading delayed when a reading's age is greater than 10 minutes. At exactly 10 minutes it remains unmarked. The temperature value and receipt time remain visible. The rule uses receipt time, not the sensor's own clock, to avoid relying on correctly set sensor clocks. No setup or dependency changes are needed. The change does not refresh a sensor or warn by email.
At h09 warning_label(age_minutes=11) returns "Reading delayed" and warning_label(age_minutes=10) returns "".
Checks at h09: 6 warning-label tests passed for the threshold, absent readings, and display text. No physical sensor or browser check occurred. h09 fully resolves #29.
Available internal links: docs/readings.md explains the age calculation; docs/display.md explains the current display; docs/testing.md contains the six-test result for h09. These documents support the facts above, but are not embedded in a pull request reader's view.

Repository: https://github.com/example-org/commute
Reviewed revision: 73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908
Project: Commute helps passengers choose a bus-and-train journey. It returns possible journeys using a published timetable. It does not use live vehicle positions or predict delays.

## Problem

Commute suggests journeys on buses and trains. It could tell a passenger to change vehicles in less than five minutes, even though the operator requires that much time to walk between stops. A passenger following that suggestion could miss the connection.

## What changed

New journey searches allow at least five minutes between one vehicle arriving and the next departing. The planner then chooses the eligible journey that arrives earliest.

## Code example

The Harbor example sets `min_transfer_seconds=300`, the default five-minute allowance:

```python
plan_trip("Harbor", min_transfer_seconds=300)
# {'bus': 17, 'train': 5, 'arrival': '08:45'}
```

Bus 17 reaches Central at 08:20. The old suggestion used Train 3 at 08:23, giving only three minutes to change. The new result uses Train 5 at 08:27 and reaches Harbor at 08:45. It gives seven minutes to change, at the cost of arriving seven minutes later.

## Why this was needed

The earliest scheduled arrival is not useful if a passenger cannot reach the connecting vehicle in time.

## Why this approach

The existing planner already compares arrival and departure times. Applying the minimum there excludes short connections before it chooses the earliest arrival, while retaining the current journey ranking.

## Setup and limits

No new setup is required. Existing callers get five minutes automatically. Callers that need another allowance can pass a nonnegative `min_transfer_seconds` value. Exactly five minutes qualifies. The rule uses published timetable times, so it cannot guarantee a connection when vehicles are delayed.

## Validation

At `73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908`, `python -m pytest tests/test_transfers.py` passed all 11 [transfer tests](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/tests/test_transfers.py). They cover gaps just below, at, and above five minutes, the default, an explicit zero override, and the Harbor journey. Running the [Harbor example](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/examples/harbor_trip.py) printed the result shown above.

The [transfer guide](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/docs/transfers.md) explains the default, override, and timetable limit. The [planner](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/src/commute/planner.py) shows where it compares the connection times. No live trip or vehicle-delay simulation was checked.

Closes #57.

## Problem

Commute admits subthreshold transfer edges into the earliest-arrival graph.

## What changed

`plan_trip` now gates edge admission on `departure - arrival >= min_transfer_seconds`, with a default of 300. The resulting itinerary still follows earliest-arrival ordering.

## Code example

```python
plan_trip("Harbor", min_transfer_seconds=300)
# {'bus': 17, 'train': 5, 'arrival': '08:45'}
```

The Harbor fixture now selects the 08:27 edge rather than the 08:23 edge after the 08:20 arrival. Its result is 08:45 rather than 08:38.

## Why this was needed

The previous admission predicate did not enforce the operator's transfer constraint.

## Why this approach

Gating connections before earliest-arrival selection retains the existing ordering among eligible itineraries and reuses the existing timestamp comparison.

## Setup and limits

No new setup is required. Callers inherit 300 or can supply a nonnegative override. The boundary is inclusive. Evaluation occurs at query time. Timetable inputs remain authoritative, with no live-position or delay model.

## Validation

At `73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908`, `python -m pytest tests/test_transfers.py` passed all 11 [transfer tests](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/tests/test_transfers.py). They cover the 299, 300, and 301 boundaries, the default, a zero override, and the Harbor selection. Running the [Harbor fixture](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/examples/harbor_trip.py) produced the result above.

The [transfer guide](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/docs/transfers.md) records the default, override, and timetable limit. The [planner](https://github.com/example-org/commute/blob/73e901c4b28d6a105f3c829ad470e6b1f5a2c908/src/commute/planner.py) shows the edge-admission comparison. No live trip or vehicle-delay simulation was checked.

Closes #57.
